newsitem.title: FINLAND: Fallout faster than facts in Finnish nuclear drill.
newsitem.headline: Fallout faster than facts in Finnish nuclear drill.

text.p: People in several eastern European countries would be bracing for radioactive fallout on Thursday, if a simulated accident at a nuclear power plant in Finland had been real.
In the one-day exercise, joined by 27 other countries in Europe and Japan and South Korea, an imaginary meltdown hit the Loviisa power station in southern Finland.
The main aim was to test the authorities' ability to get information out.
The drill was not directly targeted at the host country, although 11 years ago this month Finland was among countries hit by fallout from the world's worst nuclear accident at Chernobyl, Ukraine.

At the Finnish Centre for Radiation and Nuclear Safety, weather and radiation experts plotted the course of the imaginary "fallout" under actual weather conditions. They found the cloud this time would be heading to the south-east.

That would mean people in Estonia and eastern Russia staying indoors, perhaps giving children iodine tablets. In Poland, Belarus, Lithuania and Latvia the World Health Organisation (WHO) may have warned farmers to get ready to shelter cattle.
Keith Baverstock, a WHO representative at the dry-run, said radiation levels in the imaginary cloud would put some young children at "significant risk" of disease later in life.
"Everything is not under control," Jukka Laaksonen, head of the Finnish Centre for Radiation and Nuclear Safety admitted at a a dummy news briefing.
Relations between authorities and the media grew tense as the mock emergency unfolded.

The calm, bearded nuclear experts monitoring developments were ruffled when they had to tell the world that their early briefings had been too optimistic, according to reporters role-playing in the event.
While at early briefings they said there was a "threat" of fallout, they later acknowledged some radioactivity had been leaking from the plant even before the accident.

A special closed Internet web site carried simulated real-time media coverage of the incident, including audio and text press releases and reports by a dummy real-time news agency. But most people complained it was too slow to use.

Even the WHO's Baverstock had a similar view. "We frankly have felt we needed more, and more secure information," he said. He was forced to issue his safety recommendations solely on the basis of press reports.

Under the exercise, an unlikely cocktail of events formed over a period of days to produce the hazard. The plant abruptly lost the power to maintain its cooling systems as a gas pipeline broke, a small plane crashed into a power line, and it started annual maintenance.
The centre's deputy director, Tero Varjoranta, was calm about the problems highlighted by the role-play. "That's part of the idea," he said. "The whole point is to learn."
A post-mortem was due to start on Friday. The exercise was part of a two-year programme set up by the Nuclear Energy Agency of the Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development.
